item.title: As people begin porting games to PC, Nintendo wants to hire someone to preserve its games
item.itunes:title: As people begin porting games to PC, Nintendo wants to hire someone to preserve its games
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
Summary

  • Nintendo hires a "Digital Archivist" to preserve and organize legacy hardware and software.
  • AI decompilations are porting remakes to PC, raising legal and preservation questions.
  • I suspect Nintendo may re-release native Switch 2 ports to outcompete unofficial PC ports.

It has been a really weird year for Nintendo. It seemed like the company was going to have a big hit with the Switch 2, but we're already seeing reports that people are using AI to decompile games like The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time's remake and port them over to PC.

We've yet to see how game developers will respond to this new trend. Microsoft has already taken its stance, as it announced a studio entirely dedicated to decompilations and ports. And while Nintendo hasn't made an official claim on its stance, I suspect that its recent job advert for a digital archivist may play into it, too.

Nintendo is looking for a digital archivist to preserve its games

There are a lot of games worth keeping

So, let's start with what Nintendo has confirmed before we jump into speculation. IGN spotted a job advert on the Nintendo of America website, which has a spot ready for a "Digital Archivist, Historical Systems." It's a 12-month position in the Redmond, WA area, and the lucky candidate will get to do the following:

"We are seeking a Digital Archivist, Historical Systems to support the preservation, organization, and accessibility of historical hardware and software information. This role will design and implement a structured framework for organizing technical records, engineering documentation, source materials, and institutional knowledge related to legacy systems and platforms."

As you might expect, you need a lot of qualifications to be considered for the spot, and it pays $33-55.

Your old Nintendo 64 games are finally getting unofficial PC ports, and they run better than emulators

Retro titles are getting even better, and it's all thanks to decompilation.

3
By  Adam Conway

Nintendo may be moving to outperform the AI ports

If it doesn't, someone will

Now that we have the facts out of the way, let's explore why Nintendo is looking for someone for this role. On the surface, there are some very valid answers: Nintendo does have a digital library of titles that people can play with their Nintendo Online subscription, for instance. Plus, the excitement around The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time remake may have inspired the company to take better care of its older titles.

However, I suspect this sudden interest in organizing older titles is part of a larger push to stem the flow of AI decompilations and ports. Emulators have always been a thorn in Nintendo's side, but this poses an even bigger threat, as people are figuring out ways to port the code over to PCs and consoles without the need for an emulator.

So, how do you beat that kind of power? Simple: you outdo them. This job offering could be the start of Nintendo bringing its whole past library onto its consoles. And this time, it doesn't need to use an emulator; it could, in theory, use the same techniques people use to get Nintendo games running natively on the PC to get them on the Switch 2. Bundle them all in with a Nintendo Online subscription, and people suddenly don't have much incentive to download hundreds of decomp games on their PC.

Again, this is just me speculating, and Nintendo has neither confirmed nor denied any plans to outdo the decomp community. But I wouldn't be surprised if the company announces plans to capitalize on this new frontier.

AI slop is taking over the retro PC port scene, but these 4 Zelda projects remind me how good it still is

Ship of Harkinian, 2ship2harkinan, Dusklight, and ZeldaWWHDRecomp are all excellent ports.

3
By  Patrick O'Rourke

item.title: AMD's Ryzen 7 5700X hits $159, and it's a great option for budget PC builders
item.itunes:title: AMD's Ryzen 7 5700X hits $159, and it's a great option for budget PC builders
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
It's been a while since we've seen a processor drop to a price that actually makes sense for budget builders. The AMD Ryzen 7 5700X is currently sitting at $159 on Amazon, and if you're putting together a new desktop or upgrading an AM4 motherboard, this is the moment to grab a Zen 3 chip that still punches well above its weight.

The AMD Ryzen 7 5700X is an excellent processor with 8 Cores and 16 processing threads that provide plenty of power and speed.

What's great about the AMD Ryzen 7 5700X?

Good budget performance that works with what you already have

For $159, you're getting an 8-core, 16-thread processor built on the mature Zen 3 architecture. The base clock is 3.4 GHz, but it boosts to 4.6 GHz when your workload demands it. That's paired with 32 MB of L3 cache and a highly efficient 65-watt TDP. Unlike its 105-watt sibling, the 5700X is designed to run cool and quiet, meaning you don't need to invest in a massive aftermarket cooler to keep it in check.

This AMD CPU supports PCIe 4.0 for fast SSDs and graphics cards, and it's fully compatible with DDR4-3200 memory, which is still cheap and abundant on the used market. AMD doesn't include a stock cooler in the box, so you'll need to source one separately. But given the 65W power draw, even a budget air cooler will keep thermals in check.

Memory compatibility is another major win for budget builders. The 5700X supports dual-channel DDR4 up to 3200 MT/s, and thanks to AMD's Infinity Fabric technology, you can actually run RAM at 4000 MT/s without losing performance stability. This means you can pair it with high-end DDR4 kits, avoiding the steep prices of DDR5 modules on newer platforms.

6 "old" CPUs worth buying in 2026 because they work with the RAM you already own

Don't waste money on inflated DDR5 systems

By  Tanveer Singh

However, the real draw here is the platform longevity. Because it uses the AM4 socket, this processor is a drop-in upgrade for existing motherboards running the 500, 400, and even select 300-series chipsets.

The only trade-offs are a slightly lower boost clock and a reduced L2 cache per core, but in real-world gaming and productivity tasks, the difference is negligible. You're getting the same instruction decoding pipeline and cache latency as the much pricier chips.

At $159, the AMD Ryzen 7 5700X is easily the cheapest way to get a capable 8-core Zen 3 processor on the market right now. You can grab it directly from Amazon while stock holds out. Just make sure to clip the coupon on the store page to get the $159 discount.

item.title: I gave my local AI model access to my personal documents, and it finally became more useful than a chatbot
item.itunes:title: I gave my local AI model access to my personal documents, and it finally became more useful than a chatbot
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
Ever since chatbots came onto the map, they've gotten really efficient at working with documents. This is great for heavy workloads, but not so much for the documents you'd rather keep private, because now they end up on Google, Anthropic, or OpenAI servers. A health insurance policy nobody can make sense of, or a few months of bank statements, is where an AI could save real time, but it's also something you want to keep local.

Add XDA on Google Add as Preferred Source Follow on Google Discover

Running a local LLM does fix a privacy side, but a local model without access to your files isn't of much use; it's still just a chatbot. You want a setup that lets you get documents into the chat and lets you point the model at a local folder of private files. Here's the setup I've been using.

I don't pay for ChatGPT, Perplexity, Gemini, or Claude – I stick to my self-hosted LLMs instead

There's no point in relying on AI tools when my local LLMs can handle everything

27
By  Ayush Pande

Getting a local model to read your files

It's about picking the right runner and a model that can actually use tools

The runner is the app that loads and runs your model, and it decides how files reach the model at all. Though I've tried probably close to a dozen runners at this point, LM Studio has always been my top pick because it's so user-friendly and already has a couple of workspace features like the in-chat document upload button. If your runner doesn't have this, I recommend opting for a local AI workspace tool, like Cherry Studio or AnythingLLM, through which you can pull in your local LLM through a server.

In LM Studio, you can attach PDFs, Word docs, and text files straight into a chat. Every model has a context window, which is how much text it can hold in one conversation, so if a file fits it goes in whole. If it doesn't fit, LM Studio pulls out the parts that look relevant to your question instead.

Attaching works for one file, but most of my notes live in folders. For those I use the filesystem MCP server. MCP is a standard way of plugging tools into AI apps, and this one lets the model open and read files in folders you choose, several at a time if you need it. This is going to be necessary for any larger batches of files you want to work with but don't want to attach one by one.

None of that helps unless the model is good at calling tools. A weaker one just guesses what's in a file without opening it. LM Studio marks which models support tool use, and Qwen 3.5 9B has been the most reliable for me, but lately I've also been loving Qwythos 9B v2, which is built on the Qwen 3.5 foundation architecture, so I use them interchangeably for file work. But if your hardware can handle the newer and larger Qwen models, definitely go for that. I also have a system prompt that tells it to stick to my files and say which one an answer came from.

These 5 Docker containers turned my local AI setup into something actually useful

These underrated apps were a godsend for my productivity needs

By  Ayush Pande

Chatbots make you start over every time

Permanent access to your files solves that

Every chatbot conversation starts from zero. Asking about something personal, for example whether a procedure is covered by my health insurance, would need me to explain the plan I'm on and pasting parts of the policy, explaining my situation, and so on. Then the following week I'd have to repeat the whole thing. A local model, especially, has this problem, because it doesn't have memory like Claude. Everything I kept retyping already existed, though. It was in the policy PDF, and in notes I'd written after appointments. So, all I had to do was give them a private place to live that my local LLM could reach inside of.

Querying my files in a way a chatbot alone can't answer

This only works when the AI has your private files open

What I actually feed it is mostly health and finance documents plus my personal notes, so the screenshots here use a copy of my vault with design and research notes swapped in instead (though I do use my local LLM for design and research from time to time).

Most of my use is questions that span more than one document. For example, checking what my insurance policy says against what a claim statement actually paid out, which I'd never sit and do with two PDFs open side by side. The filesystem connection is what makes this practical, because the model can work through a whole folder without me attaching files one by one.

Then I also like to ask questions about patterns and whatever I've taken note of in the past. My notes are full of decisions I made and promptly forgot the reasoning behind, like why I switched plans or what a doctor told me. I know it's written down somewhere, just not exactly where. So the filesystem tool is great for sniffing those out because you don't need the exact file name to retrieve it.

It's also decent at turning my own material into something new, for example a short rundown of symptoms and dates to take into an appointment. I don't think a bigger model would necessarily do better at this. The cloud models I pay for have never seen these files, and getting them there would mean uploading the docs I made this setup for in the first place.

My local LLM didn't replace my $20 Claude subscription, it replaced everything I was never comfortable sending to the cloud

There are many things Qwen3.6 struggles with, but keeping my data safe isn't one of them

10
By  Abhinav Raj

Where it still acts like a chatbot

Having my files doesn't mean it always reads them properly

Smaller models sometimes answer from what they assume is in a document instead of opening it. So I still check the file it names before trusting responses with numbers in them. Context length is the other limit. A big folder or a long PDF won't fit, and when LM Studio switches to pulling out chunks it occasionally grabs the wrong section. Mentioning terms I know are in there helps. Scanned documents are their own problem, since a PDF that's just an image of a page has no text for the model to read without a separate OCR setup.

Bigger cloud models were never going to be the fix for private paperwork

Right now I'm paying for two AI subscriptions, and it turns out the model I trust the most with documents that matter the most is a free 9B one running on my own hardware. It's slower than the cloud ones for sure, but this isn't exactly work that has a deadline. And Qwen is strong enough at tool calling to be mostly reliable with the filesystem tool.

Ever since chatbots came onto the map, they've gotten really efficient at working with documents. This is great for heavy workloads, but not so much for the documents you'd rather keep private, because now they end up on Google, Anthropic, or OpenAI servers. A health insurance policy nobody can make sense of, or a few months of bank statements, is where an AI could save real time, but it's also something you want to keep local.

Add XDA on Google Add as Preferred Source Follow on Google Discover

Running a local LLM does fix a privacy side, but a local model without access to your files isn't of much use; it's still just a chatbot. You want a setup that lets you get documents into the chat and lets you point the model at a local folder of private files. Here's the setup I've been using.

I don't pay for ChatGPT, Perplexity, Gemini, or Claude – I stick to my self-hosted LLMs instead

There's no point in relying on AI tools when my local LLMs can handle everything

27
By  Ayush Pande

Getting a local model to read your files

It's about picking the right runner and a model that can actually use tools

The runner is the app that loads and runs your model, and it decides how files reach the model at all. Though I've tried probably close to a dozen runners at this point, LM Studio has always been my top pick because it's so user-friendly and already has a couple of workspace features like the in-chat document upload button. If your runner doesn't have this, I recommend opting for a local AI workspace tool, like Cherry Studio or AnythingLLM, through which you can pull in your local LLM through a server.

In LM Studio, you can attach PDFs, Word docs, and text files straight into a chat. Every model has a context window, which is how much text it can hold in one conversation, so if a file fits it goes in whole. If it doesn't fit, LM Studio pulls out the parts that look relevant to your question instead.

Attaching works for one file, but most of my notes live in folders. For those I use the filesystem MCP server. MCP is a standard way of plugging tools into AI apps, and this one lets the model open and read files in folders you choose, several at a time if you need it. This is going to be necessary for any larger batches of files you want to work with but don't want to attach one by one.

None of that helps unless the model is good at calling tools. A weaker one just guesses what's in a file without opening it. LM Studio marks which models support tool use, and Qwen 3.5 9B has been the most reliable for me, but lately I've also been loving Qwythos 9B v2, which is built on the Qwen 3.5 foundation architecture, so I use them interchangeably for file work. But if your hardware can handle the newer and larger Qwen models, definitely go for that. I also have a system prompt that tells it to stick to my files and say which one an answer came from.

These 5 Docker containers turned my local AI setup into something actually useful

These underrated apps were a godsend for my productivity needs

By  Ayush Pande

Chatbots make you start over every time

Permanent access to your files solves that

Every chatbot conversation starts from zero. Asking about something personal, for example whether a procedure is covered by my health insurance, would need me to explain the plan I'm on and pasting parts of the policy, explaining my situation, and so on. Then the following week I'd have to repeat the whole thing. A local model, especially, has this problem, because it doesn't have memory like Claude. Everything I kept retyping already existed, though. It was in the policy PDF, and in notes I'd written after appointments. So, all I had to do was give them a private place to live that my local LLM could reach inside of.

Querying my files in a way a chatbot alone can't answer

This only works when the AI has your private files open

What I actually feed it is mostly health and finance documents plus my personal notes, so the screenshots here use a copy of my vault with design and research notes swapped in instead (though I do use my local LLM for design and research from time to time).

Most of my use is questions that span more than one document. For example, checking what my insurance policy says against what a claim statement actually paid out, which I'd never sit and do with two PDFs open side by side. The filesystem connection is what makes this practical, because the model can work through a whole folder without me attaching files one by one.

Then I also like to ask questions about patterns and whatever I've taken note of in the past. My notes are full of decisions I made and promptly forgot the reasoning behind, like why I switched plans or what a doctor told me. I know it's written down somewhere, just not exactly where. So the filesystem tool is great for sniffing those out because you don't need the exact file name to retrieve it.

It's also decent at turning my own material into something new, for example a short rundown of symptoms and dates to take into an appointment. I don't think a bigger model would necessarily do better at this. 10

item.title: Someone used Claude to give GTA 2 a huge graphical makeover, so I had to try it
item.itunes:title: Someone used Claude to give GTA 2 a huge graphical makeover, so I had to try it
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
We are just about a week away from GTA 6 coming out, and it would have been perfectly normal for even GTA V or GTA IV to make the rounds in the news cycle. GTA 2, however, was not on my bingo card (or anyone's) for receiving a rejuvenation in 2026, and yet, here we are.

Add XDA on Google Add as Preferred Source Follow on Google Discover

Nvidia's RTX Remix software gives new life to old games by introducing path tracing into their rendering pipelines. That's exactly what someone used to nearly remake Grand Theft Auto 2, which, at this point, is just as old as me. After trying it out myself, it felt like playing a modern top-down game that I swear could've come out just yesterday.

GTA 2 just got the RTX Remix treatment

From basic ray tracing to a full path-traced makeover

Before someone used Claude to give GTA 2 the perfect path-tracing treatment, there was an earlier version of this project, and it was already impressive. GitHub user gebdag created the gta2-rtx-remix, taking a game designed around '90s-era hardware, and letting it realize the full potential of a modern-day RTX GPU.

Apparently, though, that wasn't enough. The new project — GTA2 RTX Upgraded — was taken much further by user kirrm3la using Claude Code, who improved the game's materials, lighting, and overall rendering in ways that make the original RTX Remix implementation look almost primitive by comparison. The result, then, isn't "GTA 2 with prettier lighting," however. What you get (and what I just played) is a 27-year-old game that feels like a completely different visual experience.

That is particularly wild because GTA 2 was the last mainline Grand Theft Auto game to use the top-down formula before GTA III dragged the series into 3D. Games like Chinatown Wars later proved Rockstar hadn't completely abandoned the formula, but GTA 2 remains one of its most recognizable 2D experiments.

And now, somehow, this 27-year-old game looks like it belongs on a modern PC. The Claude-assisted version adds physically based materials, path-traced lighting and reflections that react to the world around them, turning what was once a collection of flat sprites and simple effects into something surprisingly convincing.

Before GTA 6 comes out, I'm playing the entirety of GTA 5 completely in my web browser

Ctrl+T for Los Santos.

By  Samarveer Singh

GTA 2 looks nothing like I remember

Even the smallest details now react to the world around them

Since a huge part of the GTA games (especially the earlier ones) is driving from payphone to payphone as fast as possible, the biggest change is, of course, the cars. The Claude-assisted version gives their metal surfaces physically based rendering materials, so they no longer look like flat textures sitting on top of sprites. Paint catches light properly, glass behaves like glass, and reflections move with the environment instead of being baked into the original artwork.

The same treatment extends to the game's nastier details. Blood pools across the road now interact with the lighting, while the flashing red and blue lights from police cars and ambulances spill onto nearby surfaces. That includes other vehicles and even the player character, and together these additions make the world of Anywhere City feel far more coherent than GTA 2 ever had any business feeling.

Daytime gameplay is remarkably beautiful, yes, but GTA 2 RTX Upgraded truly shines at night. Every time I drove under a streetlamp or beside a neon-lit building, my car immediately reflected them. The reflections themselves whizzed past every car in motion, and the new lighting system was particularly impressive when I saw my car's headlights dynamically light up and reflect on civilians and buildings around me.

At this point, night gameplay in GTA 2 with the RTX Remix Upgrade mod flexing its muscles feels like playing a different game altogether, and it almost feels like a fantastic palette cleanser before GTA 6 finally drops on November 19.

You can get GTA 2 running like this yourself

The setup is surprisingly painless

Getting GTA 2 itself is probably the hardest part, simply because Rockstar has completely delisted it from its storefront. Fortunately, the project's GitHub repository points you towards the files you need, so you won't have to wander around the internet looking for a copy of a game that's a quarter-century old.

Once you have GTA 2 installed, the actual modding process is almost laughably simple. Download the original open-source RTX Remix files, extract them directly into your GTA 2 installation folder, then grab the Claude-assisted Remix files and put those into the same directory. After that, just click the GTA2 executable to get going. Thankfully, there's no elaborate mod manager, installation wizard or ritual sacrifice required.

It's not as simple as downloading an RTX Remix version of Portal or Half-Life 2 right off the Steam storefront, but it's the next best thing in terms of being frictionless.

When GTA 2 RTX Remix launches, you can immediately start experimenting with the new rendering pipeline, including full path tracing and the various graphical options RTX Remix offers. In fact, you can even enable frame generation, which is particularly amusing in a game this old. Watching GTA 2 run at a smooth 60fs with modern GPU features is probably the closest thing to overkill you can do to a top-down crime simulator from 1999.

I ran DLSS 5 on my PS2 games, and they finally looked like I remembered them

Nostalgia, meet neural rendering

11
By  Samarveer Singh

Claude Code's strangest legacy might be game modding

It's been wonderfully absurd to see the modding community embrace Claude Code and other AI coding tools to breathe new life into games that predate the hardware we run it on by decades. GTA 2 was never designed for any of this, which is precisely why seeing modern rendering techniques work on it feels so satisfying.

The bigger question is how long this particular era of AI-assisted modding can continue. Anthropic has already started placing tighter restrictions around reverse-engineering existing software, decompositions, and similar workflows. Whether that ultimately slows down projects like this or simply pushes developers towards more creative ways of working remains to be seen. For now, though, I am absolutely here for the madness.

GTA 2 RTX Upgraded

item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
A smart home that turns off the lights while you’re still sitting on the couch isn’t smart. Cheap PIR sensors only detect movement, and a ready-made presence sensor in every room adds up quickly. The Aqara Presence Sensor FP2 is listed at $80 per room. Even a Wi-Fi-based motion sensor can’t tell if you’re still there.

Add XDA on Google Add as Preferred Source Follow on Google Discover

But an ESP32 and a mmWave radar module can. With ESPHome, an ESP32-C6, and an HLK-LDR2410C module, you can make a presence sensor that can pick up your breathing, and the pair costs around $15. Here’s how I would build one for every room, and where it needs work.

4 ESP32 projects that need nothing more than the board and a USB cable

You don't need extra sensors just to build a couple of ESP32 projects

1
By  Ayush Pande

Motion sensors can’t tell you that you’re still in the room

PIR and Wi-Fi sensing both need you to move

PIR sensors work by reacting to heat moving across their view. So when you sit or lie down, they lose you. That’s the limit of Adam Conway’s $5 Zigbee build on the ESP32-C6. Wi-Fi sensing has the same gap. ESPectre turns the ESP32’s radio into a motion sensor, which works well for hallways where it has to report motion. But it can’t tell when someone is sleeping or sitting in the room.

Presence needs a sensor that picks up tiny movements. An mmWave radar sensor sends out a signal and reads the reflections, so it can pick up your chest rising and falling, even when you’re asleep. Tiny shifts in those reflections show up as movement. My colleague, Jasmine Mannan, explains why that works where PIR doesn’t. That’s what a real presence sensor needs.

An ESP32 and an mmWave module cost about $15 per room

The LD2410C talks to ESPHome over UART

The ESP32-C6 board costs about $5, and radar modules like the LD2410C are available under $10 on AliExpress. Older variants include the LD2410 and LD2410B. Still, the LD2410C has standard 254mm pin headers, Bluetooth connectivity, and a slightly larger PCB with well-spaced pins, making it easy to connect Dupont jumper wires. It also has Bluetooth for configuration through the HLKRadarTool app.

The wiring involves four connections: 5V, ground, and the UART TX and RX lines between the board and the sensor. The LD2410C’s 24GHz radio reaches about 6 meters, which is good enough for an office or a bedroom. But the same signal weakens a lot through walls, so every room needs its own sensor. That’s why the cost is per room, not per home.

With ESPHome, you can set the LD2410C’s UART to 256000 baud and add the LD2410 platform. In Home Assistant, you get the Presence entity along with moving and still target entities. I would use the moving target to turn on the lights quickly, and the still target to help decide when to turn them off.

Mount the module on the wall facing where you usually sit or sleep, and keep it away from fans or moving curtains to avoid false presence reports.

XIAO ESP32 C6

The XIAO ESP32 C6 is a great starting point for the world of ESP microcontrollers.

See at Amazon $5 at Seeed Studio

Using Bluetooth proxies to report who’s in the room

Bermuda adds identity to the radar’s yes or no

Bluetooth can also tell you who’s in the room. An ESP32 running as a Bluetooth proxy listens for BLE advertisements from phones and watches. With the Bermuda integration installed through HACS, Home Assistant estimates which room a particular device is in. Adam Conway built a Bluetooth-based presence sensor around the same idea.

However, I wouldn’t rely on that alone, because it only works if someone carries a phone or a watch. My family tends to leave their phones in drawers, so my multimodal presence sensor pairs Bluetooth with radar. In the end, radar answers whether the room is occupied, and the Bluetooth answers who is in it. The good thing is that an ESP32 board with a radar module can run Bluetooth proxy too, so you don’t need a separate board.

You need to tune radar before trusting it

The false triggers show up with still presence

An mmWave sensor is more sensitive than it looks, and you’ll need time to tune out false positives. For example, ceiling fans and moving curtains can create phantom readings, as Jasmine notes, and the radar can sometimes pick up movement through a thin wall. A sensor can get stuck reporting presence in an empty room until you adjust its thresholds.

ESPHome’s LD2410 component also has a timeout, which sets how long presence holds after the sensor stops seeing you and defaults to 5 seconds. So you will want a longer one for rooms where you sit still. Begin with default sensitivity, watch the Presence entity for a day, and then adjust one distance gate at a time.

My multimodal build’s hardware took less than an hour, and tuning out the false positives took a couple of days. I am still setting up mmWave units in the remaining rooms, so I can’t promise a smooth first night. The boards also need USB power, so each room needs a nearby power outlet, and the $15 doesn’t include the cable and adapter. If you’d rather not tune anything, a plug-and-play commercial sensor like the Aqara FP2 is easier. That’s the real trade-off with ESP32: you save money and give up some time.

I turned Wi-Fi signal into a home motion sensor using an ESP32, and it now controls my smart devices

It's what my Home Assistant server was missing all along

3
By  Ayush Pande

You can avoid overspending on presence sensors for every room

An ESP32-C6 with an LD2410 module can deliver real presence sensing on a tight per-room budget. Also, everything stays local in Home Assistant. Radar handles whether someone’s in the room, and a Bluetooth proxy identifies who’s present. The price is tuning time and pulling a power outlet in each room. I will take my time to put mmWave units in the remaining rooms, then add Bluetooth proxies where I want to know who is home.

item.title: I ran Codex inside Home Assistant, and having it next to my smart home changed how I code
item.itunes:title: I ran Codex inside Home Assistant, and having it next to my smart home changed how I code
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
I've been using AI coding agents for quite some time now, and they've made it much easier to build and experiment with projects that I wouldn't have attempted otherwise. But Home Assistant has always been a little different. Working on automations often requires you to copy YAML files, explain how different devices and entities are connected, and go back and forth between the agent and Home Assistant to test changes.

Add XDA on Google Add as Preferred Source Follow on Google Discover

More recently, I started using the computer use feature in Codex to let it inspect my Home Assistant setup and handle some of these tasks itself, but that burns through tokens very quickly. A better solution I discovered just last month was an add-on that lets you run Codex directly inside Home Assistant, with access to its config files.

Codex makes a lot more sense inside Home Assistant

It can work with your existing configuration

One thing about Home Assistant is that even a relatively simple automation can involve several moving parts. You might have a motion sensor controlling a light, a separate presence-based routine, and another script that changes how the same light behaves at night. When something goes wrong, or you want to make changes, you need to account for how all these things work together.

The HA Codex add-on gives you a terminal that runs within Home Assistant, with read and write access to its configuration directory. Codex can go through your existing YAML files, inspect automations and scripts, and understand how you've organized things.

For example, if I want to improve a lighting automation, I can ask Codex to inspect the relevant files first. Codex can look at the triggers, conditions, and actions, identify other scripts that might be involved, and suggest changes based on what's already there. That's a lot more convenient than asking a coding agent to generate an automation from scratch and then figuring out how to make it fit into my setup.

However, access to config files doesn't give it live information about device states or automation history. You still need to provide that context when necessary. And you could achieve similar file access with Codex running on another computer.

n8n saved me more time this year than any AI tool, and most of my workflows don't use AI at all

n8n is hands down the best tool for automation.

1
By  Anurag Singh

Getting Codex running inside Home Assistant

You only need an add-on

The easiest way to get Codex running inside Home Assistant is through the HA Codex add-on, available on GitHub. It's a community-developed project, so you won't find it in Home Assistant's default app store. You'll need to add its repository manually.

To install it, open Home Assistant and head to Settings -> Apps -> App Store. From there, open the repository management menu and add the following URL:

https://github.com/ambient-home-systems/ha-codex

Once you've added the repository, HA Codex should appear in the app store. Install it, start the add-on, and enable the Show in sidebar option. You can now open Codex directly from Home Assistant's sidebar, just like any other app.

The first time you launch it, you'll need to authenticate. The easiest option is to select Log in with a different device, which gives you a URL and a temporary code. Open the link on another device, sign in with your ChatGPT account, and complete the authorization. You'll need an account with Codex access, although the add-on also supports API-key authentication if that option is available.

You can choose which model Codex uses, adjust its reasoning effort, and enable session persistence, so your terminal stays active when you navigate elsewhere in Home Assistant. I would also leave Skip command approvals disabled, since Codex has permission to modify your configuration files.

The add-on also has an optional setting called Allow Home Assistant control actions. You can enable it to let Codex validate your configuration and request supported reload actions, which is useful when testing changes without manually reloading everything.

I put Codex to work on my smart home

Building and fixing automations became easier

One of the first things worth trying with Codex is improving an automation that already exists. For example, I have presence-based routines that control my lights depending on whether I'm home and the time of day. I can ask Codex to examine the existing logic, check for conflicting conditions, and suggest changes. It can also show me exactly what it wants to modify before I approve anything.

If an automation stops working after a change, Codex can also inspect the YAML, check for syntax errors, and look at any scripts or other configuration files involved. Of course, there are limits to what it can diagnose from the files alone. If a motion sensor isn't reporting correctly or an automation isn't triggering, I'll still need to check Home Assistant's traces and device history to figure out what's happening.

The add-on becomes particularly useful when you enable Home Assistant control actions. After making a change, Codex can run a configuration check and reload supported components, including automations and scripts. You can then test the updated automation in Home Assistant without necessarily restarting the entire system. I wouldn't let it make these changes without approval, though, because even a small mistake could affect other routines.

One thing to keep in mind

There is one limitation worth mentioning. The add-on requires Home Assistant OS, so if you're running Home Assistant in Docker, you can't install it directly. You'd need to run Home Assistant OS instead, potentially in a virtual machine. A VM isn't necessary if you're already running Home Assistant OS on dedicated hardware.

After a month with VS Code's new agents window, I stopped caring about Cursor

VS Code now has it all.

The easiest way to get Codex running inside Home Assistant is through the HA Codex add-on, available on GitHub. It's a community-developed project, so you won't find it in Home Assistant's default app store. You'll need to add its repository manually.

The first time you launch it, you'll need to authenticate. The easiest option is to select Log in with a different device, which gives you a URL and a temporary code. You'll need an account with Codex access, although the add-on also supports API-key authentication if that option is available.

You can choose which model Codex uses, adjust its reasoning effort, and enable session persistence, so your terminal stays active when you navigate elsewhere in Home Assistant. I would also leave Skip command approvals disabled, since Codex has permission to modify your configuration files.

The add-on also has an optional setting called Allow Home Assistant control actions. You can enable it to let Codex validate your configuration and request supported reload actions, which is useful when testing changes without manually reloading everything.

There is one limitation worth mentioning. The add-on requires Home Assistant OS, so if you're running Home Assistant in Docker, you can't install it directly. item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
Graphics cards are more than just the big silicon GPU die on them, and while that makes up a huge part of the performance, there are lots of other factors that determine how far your card can go. Somewhere on your card lives a little flash chip that holds the VBIOS, and for the vast majority of GPU owners, this goes untouched, and that's mostly because of the inherent risk of flashing it and potentially bricking the card.

Add XDA on Google Add as Preferred Source Follow on Google Discover

When the reward is a few more points in a benchmark score, that risk-reward ratio doesn't make much sense, but with the help of some clever modders, RTX 50 series cards can now be loaded with a modified VBIOS without the need to flash anything. Skipping the flash takes the classic bricked-card scenario off the table, but the limits being edited exist to protect the hardware, and the method only works for as long as NVIDIA’s drivers allow it.

These small toggles can play a large part in your system's overall performance

By  Ty Sherback

What a VBIOS controls, and why people want to change it at all

It's like your motherboard's BIOS, only just for the GPU

Every graphics card carries firmware known as the VBIOS, and it's responsible for dictating how your card behaves. It sets the card's ceilings: power draw, voltage, clocks, fan speed, and other numbers live there. Board partners ship different values, which is a big reason a premium model can run a higher power target than a budget model with the same GPU. Some premium cards are known to ship multiple VBIOS options on the same card, allowing enthusiast users to use a physical switch to tap into a version of the firmware with even higher limits.

Familiar tuning apps like MSI Afterburner, EVGA Precision X1, or nvidia-smi on Linux, all work inside of those limits set by the VBIOS. They can't push the ceiling any higher than the firmware allows. Editing the VBIOS moves the limits themselves, and that cuts both ways. Overclockers want higher ceilings, but plenty of owners want lower floors for quieter, cooler, or more power-efficient machines.

5 GPU myths that manufacturers still take advantage of

Manufacturers use them to sell you more expensive components, not just GPUs.

By  Tanveer Singh

Why flashing has progressively become more difficult

Nvidia wants to lock things down

Since the GeForce 900 series, Nvidia has been signing their firmware and using an on-board security processor to ensure no unauthorized images can be booted on the card. There have been tools released that could bypass the signature cards on older cards, but on anything newer than around the RTX 20-series, the most realistic option was cross-flashing another vendor's VBIOS that's signed, but that, of course, comes with significant risk.

A breakthrough for overclockers and tinkerers

The new approach for modifying the limits on a GPU skips the VBIOS chip entirely. In Windows, the edited image sits in the GPU’s driver settings within the registry, and the driver reads it in place of the chip’s copy when the card starts. On Linux, a loader patches Nvidia’s open-source kernel modules so the GSP, an onboard processor Nvidia GPUs have included since the RTX 20 series, starts the card with the edited image instead.

Either way, if the image is rejected, the card falls back to its stock VBIOS. Removing the override returns everything to normal, and that override can also persist across reboots, though a driver update can wipe it. Some settings will always stay out of reach, like memory timings.

The tools that enable users to do these softmods have been popping up all over GitHub, but the most complete toolkit comes from a developer known as Panchovix, who built on an earlier override mod done by overclock.net user pantsoftime. It has three parts, all now open source: an editor that changes values in a copy of your own card’s VBIOS, plus separate loaders for Windows and Linux. Editing goes deepest on RTX 50 cards, covering power, voltage, clock, current, and fan settings. RTX 40 and 30 cards are more limited, and RTX 20 support is experimental at this time.

The other big name is mVolt+, which made headlines back in August for pushing RTX 50 series cards far beyond their rated power. It, too, now has a BIOS override, which writes the same registry values as Panchovix's Windows loader.

4 apps I couldn't live without on my small form factor PC

A ton of power packed into a tiny package.

By  Jacob Roach

Nvidia still controls the cat-and-mouse game

Driver updates can break these tools, and they have

As you'd expect, none of this is supported by Nvidia, and driver updates have already broken parts of these tools. Not long after mVolt+ unlocked higher power on RTX 50 cards, a driver update made that control black-screen the card, and a later update restricted some of its voltage and current controls, even through the BIOS override. mVolt+ has since found new routes through its own override to restore them, though the situation is very active. From one driver version to the next, there's no guarantee that these tools keep working in their entirety.

My RTX Spark laptop rendered a Blender scene too big for an RTX 5090, and a local LLM on the same machine built it

It's not faster than an RTX 5090, but the additional VRAM makes for some cool tricks.

12
By  Adam Conway

Who should probably leave this alone

The limits within the VBIOS are there for a reason

Skipping the flashing part does eliminate the risk of bricking the card due to a bad flash, but it doesn't remove the risk of doing irreversible damage to the card itself. Power, current, and voltage limits protect components like the voltage regulators and the power connector. The 12V-2x6 connector on high-end cards is rated for 600W, and an RTX 5090 is already rated at 575W, which leaves very little headroom for a raised limit at the high-end.

Even for cards like the RTX 5080 and under, the limits set by Nvidia are likely as high as made sense to begin with, since the payoff in games is modest. Testing of mVolt+ found small gains from raised power limits on some cards, and lower frame rates when voltage was pinned at its maximum. These tools are primarily going to be for the tinkerers and overclockers that like to drag race their cards in benchmarks, not necessarily those who want a few extra frames while gaming.

I let the NVIDIA App overclock my GPU, and it left me impressed

For a "conservative" OC tool, the NVIDIA App gave me remarkable results

7
By  Samarveer Singh

These tools are still invaluable

The real breakthrough is the reversibility that these tools offer. Previously, testing a VBIOS meant having to touch the chip every time you wanted to make a change, and now, it can be edited, tested, and removed without needing to roll the dice every time. The process is safer, but these tweaks are still niche for a reason, and the limits are there to protect the average user who doesn't really need that extra few percent. That's what tools like MSI Afterburner are for, and plenty can be done with those to squeeze more performance out of your card without the risk of hardware damage.

item.title: The ESP32 is replacing Raspberry Pis in my home lab for simple jobs, and it costs far less to run
item.itunes:title: The ESP32 is replacing Raspberry Pis in my home lab for simple jobs, and it costs far less to run
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
Raspberry Pi was an impressive product when it launched in 2012 through the Raspberry Pi Foundation. Its goal was to make computing and programming more accessible, providing an affordable single-board computer (SBC) that anyone could experiment with. It worked, with millions of Raspberry Pi computers sold worldwide. Compared to a desktop PC, the Raspberry Pi is considerably less powerful, but that's part of its appeal, especially when it comes to the smart home and home lab. It can handle all sorts of low-power tasks without requiring expensive hardware or much electricity. But so too can a microcontroller like the ESP32, and I've increasingly found myself turning to these tiny boards instead.

Add XDA on Google Add as Preferred Source Follow on Google Discover

Raspberry Pi is great for the home lab

But so too is an army of ESP32-built devices

The Raspberry Pi 5 is powered by a quad-core ARM CPU and offers up to 16GB of RAM to run full-size Linux distributions. You could fire up Arch Linux, install Home Assistant and some other self-hosted apps, and call it a day. The Raspberry Pi will handle many lightweight services without much trouble. But things get interesting when you want to create low-powered sensors and other devices that add functionality to the smart home and home lab. This is where an ESP32 can make much more sense, especially when you don't need an entire operating system running in the background.

A Raspberry Pi 5 can consume around 5 to 15 watts depending on the workload and connected peripherals, though I've usually found mine to hover towards the lower end of the spectrum. As for an ESP32, it uses a fraction of this power. These microcontrollers can run from small batteries, provided the voltage is regulated appropriately, and can achieve exceptionally low power consumption when configured to enter deep sleep between tasks. They're also incredibly versatile and can be paired with a whole host of sensors, attachments, and completely custom circuitry.

Even if you have very little confidence or knowledge when it comes to electronics, ESP32 starter kits come with guides and many of the components required to create something unique. This is what I applaud the Raspberry Pi for, since I know plenty of people who have purchased a Raspberry Pi kit over the years and played around with attaching components, running services, and even learning programming languages. The ESP32 feels like a natural continuation of that experimentation, bringing a similarly accessible approach to microcontrollers.

And the costs can be considerably lower. A Raspberry Pi typically needs a suitable power supply and storage, and you might also want a case or other accessories. An ESP32 development board can cost just a few pounds, leaving plenty of room in the budget for sensors, displays, and other components. When you're building a collection of devices throughout the home, those savings can quickly add up. Depending on what you're replacing, it's possible to save hundreds of pounds compared to buying numerous fully assembled commercial smart-home accessories.

I stopped buying Raspberry Pis after testing budget friendly mini PCs, and here's why you should too

I tested three mini PCs.

By  Jasmine Mannan

ESP32 is perfect for DIY home lab projects

ESPHome makes creating smart devices surprisingly easy

One of the best things about ESP32 hardware is how easily it integrates with Home Assistant. ESPHome allows you to configure compatible microcontrollers using YAML, with support for numerous sensors, displays, and other components. While this does mean I don't need to dive into C or some other language, YAML is also fairly convoluted at times, especially if you're unfamiliar with mastering the fine art that is indentation.

The first time I finally unboxed an ESP32 kit, I connected a compatible sensor, configured the relevant pins and components, and flashed the firmware, and I had a device that can communicate with your smart home. The entire process took around 30 minutes. I've even used an ESP32 to create a small energy-monitoring display for my Home Assistant installation. It can show information such as current solar generation, battery state of charge, household consumption, and grid usage using a small OLED screen. item.itunes:title: One of my favorite Jellyfin clients for Android TV just got even better with its latest update
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
Jellyfin is a versatile platform for serving your media to screens throughout your home. Community enthusiasts have created several plugins and clients that improve the viewing experience for your movies and shows across multiple platforms. One of the best for Android/Google TV devices is Wholphin, which has improved with a recent update.

Add XDA on Google Add as Preferred Source Follow on Google Discover

It is a Plex-inspired, straightforward client for playing self-hosted media on the big screen. It does one thing and does it very well — displaying your media library. It has recently been improved, and it's getting even better by giving me more control over how I display content on the big screen.

A client that's been a favorite Android TV option

It's Plex-inspired and not just another Jellyfin client

One appealing quality of alternative Jellyfin clients like Wholphin is that it makes the transition easier for Plex-to-Jellyfin converts. The client isn't just a fork of the official Jellyfin version; it was written from scratch and allows more choice. It has a familiar interface and offers plenty of customization and playback engine options. It does more than stream your media to devices in the house. Wholphin provides more control over watching and browsing your media.

With more choice and headroom for your media, it complements the Android ecosystem better. The home screen centers on your media library. It offers tangible advantages, including customizing rows of movies and shows, selecting artwork, collection pins, playlists, and more. It's more than a nicer interface; it puts the content you watch most at your fingertips. It also supports ExoPlayer, an Android-native playback option. Plus, it includes MPV as an alternative fallback if ExoPlayer struggles with files.

Jellyfin finally feels good on my TV, but I had to stop using the default client

Wholphin is the Jellyfin client Android TV should have shipped with.

15
By  Samarveer Singh

Improve your video viewing experience

A slew of new features for better picture and more

Most changes in this version are under the hood, rather than a complete app overhaul. Still, the improvements can boost picture quality for your movies and shows, enhance audio and subtitles, improve Live TV, and more. The new automatic HDR detection is tucked into Wholphin's advanced settings section. If automatic HDR detection doesn't get the picture right for your display, you can force HDR10, HDR10+, or individual Dolby Vision settings.

Now, I can override automatic HDR or Dolby Vision detection for certain content in my media library. I can adjust the max bitrate without leaving the viewing experience. I can also carry audio and subtitle selections between show episodes. The in-player bitrate tool is an improvement since I don't have to leave the video to adjust it. There's also an optional server plugin that lets admins preconfigure Wholphin's home page and set up Serr integration.

The plugin is easy to configure with a short YAML script. Once that was set up, I could add my Serr address by signing in to my account to connect it. It's more of a technical addition to the client than a redesigned home screen option. I used it to connect the app to Serr running in Docker on another PC. It's optional, and not everyone needs it. However, it is useful if you have Serr running and want more content discovery through the Wholphin interface.

Since I set up my tuner to watch live TV, I appreciate the improvements and fixes for HDHomeRun Live TV direct playback. The issue affecting direct playback from the tuner is now fixed. Like many other updates, this one doesn't change the Live TV interface, but it's a worthwhile improvement for Jellyfin users with the SiliconDust TV tuner.

I ditched Jellyfin’s official app for alternative clients that fit my devices better

It's good there's choice in Jellyfin clients that best suit specific devices.

By  Brian Burgess

Keeping track of my music collection

Smaller improvements for self-hosted CD rips

I've been working through my workflow of digitizing my CDs to lossless audio and adding the FLAC files to Jellyfin, so I appreciate that the update includes a few music updates. I can choose which bands appear on the Artists page in the music section. When I open the music section, I can choose between artists and album artists, which gives me more control over my music collection.

In addition, album cards display the album title under the artist name. It's a minor visual change, but it gives me better context for the color grid. Especially when the album cover artwork is incorrect or missing. When that happens, it's harder to find my albums while browsing, but the identifier makes it easier to keep track of my CDs. There aren't any audio improvements, but it does make it easier to identify my music.

I ripped my CDs again after 20 years of old MP3s, and it's the best audio upgrade I've made in ages

I got rid of crappy sounding MP3's and upgraded my audio to better quality FLAC rips.

17
By  Brian Burgess

The best Jellyfin client for Android TV devices continues to improve

Most updates happen behind the scenes, but they help me watch movies and shows and listen to music. The ability to change the bitrate while watching content is a visible and welcome addition. There isn't a major redesign to the interface, since it's already good as-is — straightforward media playback with a familiar design. The unseen improvements make it a more solid foundation for playing my content from my Jellyfin server on Android TV devices.
